title: Insomnia Triples Breast Cancer Risk in Women Under 50. A Study of 19 Million People Just Presented the Numbers at ASCO.
excerpt: The largest real-world analysis of its kind found that young women diagnosed with insomnia faced up to three times the risk of hormone-related cancers. Bowel cancer risk nearly doubled regardless of gender.
body:
A study of 19 million people aged 18 to 50, presented this week at the American Society of Clinical Oncology's annual meeting in Chicago, has found that women diagnosed with insomnia are three times more likely to develop breast cancer within five years.

The research, conducted by scientists from Jefferson Health in New Jersey and the Ochsner MD Anderson Cancer Centre in Louisiana, analysed medical data collected between January 2021 and January 2026. More than 413,000 participants had a formal insomnia diagnosis.

## The Numbers Are Stark

Women with insomnia faced a threefold increase in breast cancer risk. Uterine cancer risk nearly doubled. Ovarian cancer risk rose by 57 per cent. All three are hormone-related cancers — and the pattern held after adjusting for known risk factors.

Bowel cancer risk also rose sharply. Insomniacs of both genders were nearly twice as likely to be diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Between the early 1990s and 2018, bowel cancer cases among people aged 25 to 49 in the UK rose by 22 per cent. The new findings suggest poor sleep may be one of the missing drivers behind that trend.

Notably, there was no significant link between insomnia and hormone-related cancers in men — no increased risk of testicular or prostate cancer.

## Why Sleep Disruption May Fuel Cancer

The researchers believe the mechanism runs through hormone signalling. Chronic insomnia disrupts the circadian clock, which regulates everything from melatonin production to oestrogen metabolism. When the clock breaks, hormone levels become erratic — and in women, that hormonal chaos may create conditions that allow tumour cells to proliferate.

"Insomnia increases in incidence and prevalence each year, and with it come likelihoods of circadian disruption, immune dysregulation, and altered hormone signalling," the research team wrote.

Dr David Garley, director of the Better Sleep Clinic, added a practical dimension. "When you aren't sleeping well, it's quite difficult to be healthy," he said. "It's harder to engage with weight management — appetite increases if you aren't sleeping well. Insulin sensitivity decreases, and people don't tend to do as much exercise."

The downstream effects compound. Poor sleep leads to weight gain. Weight gain increases oestrogen production. Higher oestrogen feeds hormone-sensitive cancers. It is a cascade, and insomnia may be the first domino.

## What This Means for South Asian Women

South Asian women face a particular convergence of risks. A 2026 study in the Journal of the American Heart Association found that South Asian women already have nearly double the prevalence of prediabetes by age 45 compared to women of other ethnic backgrounds — a condition linked to insulin resistance, which itself worsens with poor sleep.

Cultural factors add pressure. Many South Asian women in the diaspora juggle demanding work schedules with family caregiving responsibilities that extend across generations and time zones. Late-night calls to India, early-morning school runs, and the emotional labour of maintaining family bonds across continents all erode sleep quality.

The researchers at ASCO were careful to note the limitations: this is an association study, not a proof of causation. It is possible that early-stage cancers themselves cause sleep disruption rather than the other way around. But the scale of the dataset — 19 million people — and the consistency of the pattern across multiple cancer types make this more than a statistical artefact.

## The Actionable Takeaway

Simon Vincent, chief scientific officer at Breast Cancer Now, said the findings warranted further investigation but that "small actions that everyone can take to reduce risk are staying physically active, limiting alcohol, being breast aware and attending screening appointments when invited."

For South Asian women in the diaspora, the specific action item is simpler and harder: take sleep seriously. Not as a luxury. Not as something that happens after everything else is done. As a clinical priority that may directly affect cancer risk.

If insomnia persists for more than three months, it is worth discussing with a doctor — not just for quality of life, but because the data now suggests the stakes may be considerably higher than anyone previously understood.
